stimulus_db: Technological improvements will enable food production to increase as populations increase. However, increases in food production will be negligible unless societies become more centralized so that all factors contributing to the production of food can be better coordinated. But, historically, the more centralized a society was, the greater the percentage of its people who perished if and when it collapsed. Thus, increasing the centralization of societies in an effort to increase food production via better technology will merely exacerbate the disasters associated with societal collapse.
stem_db: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices_db.A: The more centralized a society is, the greater its need for increased food production.
choices_db.B: Not every problem associated with the collapse of a centralized society would be prevented by technological improvements.
choices_db.C: The rate at which the world’s population is growing will continue to increase indefinitely.
choices_db.D: The production of food can be increased only by improved technology.
choices_db.E: Societies have become more centralized as technology has improved.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body: Technology could raise food production, but only negligibly unless societies centralize. Historically, the more centralized a society, the more of its people died when it collapsed. So centralizing to boost food production will make collapses worse.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: Pause and infer. Technology brings more food, but the centralization it needs makes collapse deadlier. So technology doesn't remove the dangers of collapse. If anything, the route to more food makes them worse.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Technology won't prevent every problem that comes with a centralized society's collapse.

notes.body: This is the most popular wrong answer. The passage ties centralization to deaths *in a collapse*, not to a greater need for food. Food production is what drives centralization, not the other way around.
Centralizing for more food makes collapses worse, so technology plainly doesn't fix every collapse problem. "Not every" asks for very little.
Population growth continuing "indefinitely" is far beyond anything here.
The passage gives no history of centralization rising with technology. It talks about what *would* happen.
